#LARPItTillYouMakeIt
summary: A browser-based jukebox that lets people see and hear how Earth’s surface temperature changed from 1980 to 2025. Visitors can play a timeline of global temperature anomalies, listen to the colors in a latitude band, and compare the same region across two years. The project addresses the Earth Information Jukebox challenge by pairing NASA maps with sounds generated as visitors explore. A global average gives listeners one note per year, while the latitude scans let them hear geographic differences and check what they heard against the maps.
details:
We built Earth Tune Studio for the Earth Information Jukebox challenge so visitors can hearand see how Earth’s surface temperature changed from 1980 to 2025. Inside the 3D studio, visitors open the monitor, choose a year, and listen to a note generated from NASA’s global temperature data while viewing that year’s map.

In History, selecting 2024 plays a note, based on a global temperature anomaly. An anomaly measures how much warmer or cooler a period was than the 1951–1980 average. Selecting 2025 brings up its map and plays a slightly lower note.

In Frame Scan, visitors can listen to one of five latitude bands. The browser samples the map pixels in the selected band and groups their colors into cooler, near-baseline, and warmer categories. Each category has a distinct sound, and a category that covers a larger share of the valid sampled pixels plays for longer. Compare A/B lets visitors hear the same band in two years. In the ten-question Quiz & Proof, they can listen, make a prediction, and check their answer against the pixel shares shown in the app.

We chose the jukebox format so learners could decide what to hear, replay a comparison, and use the maps and numbers to check what the sound represents. We considered how the controls would work on smaller screens and how to explain what the comparisons measure. The historical maps show running averages, while the 2025 map uses annual averages for each grid cell. The regional comparisons describe the colors in the displayed maps, which represent different averaging periods.

We built the interface with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and modeled the studio in Blender. Three.js renders the room and globe, Canvas samples the map pixels, and the Web Audio API synthesizes the sounds in the browser. We used Node.js to serve the project during local development.
